EXAMPLES_GALLERY_INTRO: Each example ships a ready-to-Run canvas — pick one and the editor opens straight on the Visual tab.
EXAMPLE_DEMO_DESC: Counter + heartbeat + stepper + 7-segment display. Every visual widget wired up at once.
EXAMPLE_COUNTER_DESC: Two 7-segment digits counting 00 → 99 with an overflow LED on rollover. Toggle the TICK switch to advance.
EXAMPLE_TRAFFIC_DESC: Three-state Moore machine cycling RED → GREEN → YELLOW. Watch the state register on the LED array.
EXAMPLE_SHIFT_DESC: Eight individual LEDs, each wired to one bit of an 8-bit register via slice syntax. Flip SI + watch the pattern walk left.
EXAMPLE_DIP_ADDER_DESC: Two 4-switch DIP banks feed a 4-bit adder; the 5-bit sum lands on a yellow LED array. Each switch is wired raw to one input bit.
EXAMPLE_MATRIX_DESC: 9-bit shift register cycles a plus-sign pattern across a 3×3 LED matrix. Flip STEP to advance the pattern one column.
EXAMPLE_RGB_DESC: Three 9-bit LFSRs drive the R/G/B planes of a 3×3 RGB matrix. Reset restarts the seed; STEP advances one cycle.
EXAMPLE_BUZZER_DESC: A 3-switch selector picks a note from the C-major octave (C4..C5); the design generates the square wave on one raw buzzer pin, gated by ENABLE. Watch it pulse in the Visual tab or in the waveform.
EXAMPLE_KEYPAD_DESC: A 4x4 matrix keypad scanned in raw VHDL: the design drives the rows, reads the columns, debounces the press, and shows the key on a raw hex 7-segment.
EXAMPLE_LCD_NAME: Example · HELLO on an HD44780 LCD
EXAMPLE_LCD_DESC: Writes "HELLO KMILA" to a 16x2 LCD over the real HD44780 4-bit bus: the design sequences RS/E and the DB4..DB7 nibbles itself. Watch the bus in the waveform.
EXAMPLE_DOTMATRIX_DESC: Scrolls "HELLO KMILA" across an 8×8 LED matrix with no driver chip: the design scans the columns and drives the row lines from its own font ROM.
EXAMPLE_LCD_RAWPANEL_DESC: Drives a bare LCD dot-matrix with the HD44780 removed: the design scans the COM backplane and drives the SEG lines from its own glyph ROM — everything the controller usually hides.
PROJECTS_SAMPLE_DESCRIPTION: A pre-wired demo design — counter + heartbeat + stepper. Switches, buttons, LEDs already bound on the Visual tab. Open it, hit Run.

PROJECTS_SAMPLE_CONFIG_DESCRIPTION: Clock + reset pulse + RUN/DIR switches + NUDGE pulse — ready to simulate the demo board.

HOME_TITLE: Kmila-9s: A Multiplatform VHDL Learning and Debugging Tool
HOME_SUBTITLE: An application for learning and debugging VHDL code without requiring physical hardware.
HOME_OVERVIEW_P1: Kmila-9s is a multiplatform desktop application, running in a local environment, aimed at debugging VHDL (VHSIC Hardware Description Language) code. Its objective is to facilitate the analysis of programs through simulation and interactive visualization of digital signals, clock cycles, and port states.
HOME_OVERVIEW_P2: The project aims to support the academic learning of digital design for FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays), offering a free and open-source tool that strengthens educational practices and allows for a practical understanding of the logic of digital systems without requiring physical hardware.
HOME_FEATURE_VISUALIZATION_DESC: Observe the states of signals, ports, and internal variables at any time.
HOME_FEATURE_CROSSPLATFORM_DESC: Runs on Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, iPadOS, and Linux (via web).
HOME_FEATURE_OFFLINE_DESC: Works locally without an internet connection.
HOME_FEATURE_PRELAB_DESC: Prepare for physical lab sessions in advance.
HOME_FEATURE_ACCESSIBILITY_DESC: Study from any computer or mobile device.
HOME_FEATURE_PROTOTYPING_DESC: Validate designs faster than with traditional methods.
HOME_GITHUB_TEXT: Find more about the project on our GitHub repository.

GATE_AND_SUMMARY: Output is 1 only when every input is 1.
GATE_AND_DESC: Boolean conjunction. The output reflects the logical AND of its inputs (y = a · b). Used to detect when multiple conditions are simultaneously true — e.g. gating a signal with an enable, masking specific bits of a vector, or building wider logic.
GATE_NAND_SUMMARY: Inverted AND: output is 0 only when every input is 1.
GATE_NAND_DESC: Logical NAND (NOT AND). The bubble at the output flips an AND's result. Notable property: NAND is universal — any other gate can be built out of NANDs alone, which is why CMOS standard-cell libraries usually have NAND as the densest primitive.
GATE_OR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when any input is 1.
GATE_OR_DESC: Boolean disjunction (y = a + b). Used to merge signals — "this OR that" — and to build alarm / event logic. Like NAND, NOR is also universal, but OR by itself is one of the two basic Boolean operators.
GATE_NOR_SUMMARY: Inverted OR: output is 1 only when every input is 0.
GATE_NOR_DESC: Logical NOR (NOT OR). Universal, like NAND — any logic can be built from NORs alone. Common in standard-cell libraries and in hardware where inverting outputs is naturally free (CMOS).
GATE_XOR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when exactly one input is 1.
GATE_XOR_DESC: Logical exclusive OR — true when the inputs differ (y = a ⊕ b). Building block for adders (sum bit), parity checkers, encryption (one-time-pad XOR), and bit-flipping. An XOR with one input tied to 1 acts as a controllable inverter.
GATE_XNOR_SUMMARY: Output is 1 when both inputs are equal.
GATE_XNOR_DESC: Logical exclusive NOR — true when the inputs match (y = a ≡ b). Useful as a per-bit equality test; an XNOR over each bit followed by an AND across results gives vector-equality (the EQ comparator we synthesise from the `=` operator).
GATE_NOT_SUMMARY: Output is the logical inverse of the input.
GATE_NOT_DESC: Single-input gate. y = ¬a — flips 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. The smallest Boolean primitive. Used to build everything from NAND/NOR by combining with AND/OR; in active-low interfaces (reset_n, write_enable_n) the inverter is what makes the polarity work out.
GATE_BUF_DESC: Single-input cell that just forwards its input (y = a). In real silicon, buffers exist to drive long wires (signal restoration), to sit in a fan-out tree, or to add a small deliberate delay. In our schematic, BUFs are emitted whenever an internal gate's output needs to be "renamed" onto a declared port or signal — they make the connection between the gate and the named net visible as a wire.
GATE_BUF_NOTE: BUFs are hidden in the Synthesis and Debug views — there they're folded away and the wire goes directly from the driving gate to the target port. Naive view keeps them so the source-line groupings stay literal.
GATE_MUX_SUMMARY: Picks one of several inputs based on a selector.
GATE_MUX_DESC: Two-input MUX: y = s ? d1 : d0. Wider MUXes select among 2^n inputs with n select bits. Multiplexers implement decision logic — every `if/then/else` and `case` statement in VHDL becomes a MUX (or a tree of them) after synthesis. They're also how registers implement load-enable: the MUX picks between "new value" and "hold" based on the enable signal.
GATE_DFF_SUMMARY: Stores one bit, sampled on the active clock edge.
GATE_DFF_DESC: Edge-triggered storage element. On each rising edge of CLK, the value at D is captured and held at Q until the next edge. Between edges Q is stable regardless of D activity. Foundational building block of synchronous design — every register, every pipeline stage, every state machine state-bit is one or more DFFs. Combine with a MUX in front of D to get an enabled register; with a 2-input MUX selecting `'0' / D` to get a synchronous reset.
GATE_DFF_NOTE: The Edge attribute on this cell tells you whether it samples on rising_edge or falling_edge.
GATE_CONST_SUMMARY: Fixed value driver — '0', '1', or a literal vector.
GATE_CONST_DESC: Constant nets show up as small labels rather than gates. Common in synthesis output: every `'0'`, `'1'`, `"0000"`, or `(others => '0')` literal in the source becomes a constant-driver net. Tying a MUX input to a constant is how synchronous reset paths are built (`d <= '0' when reset = '1' else next_value`).
GATE_ADD_DESC: Renders the `+` operator. Internally, an adder is a chain of full-adders (XOR for the sum bit, AND/OR for the carry), but we keep it as one opaque cell by default — an 8-bit ripple-carry adder is ~50 gates and would dominate the diagram. The exporter's "expand arithmetic" toggle (planned) breaks this down to gates.
GATE_SUB_DESC: Renders the `-` operator. Built from an adder plus a row of NOTs and a carry-in of 1 (two's complement: a − b = a + (¬b) + 1). Kept opaque for the same reason as ADD.
GATE_MUL_DESC: Renders the `*` operator. Multipliers in hardware are large structures (an n×n multiplier is roughly n² half-adders). Often mapped to dedicated DSP slices on FPGAs rather than synthesised as logic gates.
GATE_DIV_DESC: Renders the `/` operator. Hardware division is expensive and slow — many designs avoid it or restrict it to multi-cycle operations.
GATE_MOD_DESC: Renders the `mod` operator. Hardware-wise this is essentially a divider that exposes the remainder. Cheap when the divisor is a power of two (just slice off the low bits).
GATE_POW_DESC: Renders the `**` operator. Rare in synthesisable VHDL; usually only seen with constant exponents (which the synthesiser unrolls into a chain of multipliers).
GATE_SHL_SUMMARY: Shifts the input vector left by N bits.
GATE_SHL_DESC: VHDL `sll` (logical) fills with 0; `sla` (arithmetic) fills with the rightmost bit. Equivalent to multiplication by 2^N when the shift amount is a constant. Implemented in hardware as a barrel shifter (a tree of 2-to-1 MUXes).
GATE_SHR_SUMMARY: Shifts the input vector right by N bits.
GATE_SHR_DESC: VHDL `srl` (logical) fills with 0; `sra` (arithmetic) fills with the sign bit. Equivalent to integer division by 2^N for unsigned (`srl`) or signed (`sra`) values.
GATE_ROL_SUMMARY: Cyclically rotates the input vector left.
GATE_ROL_DESC: Bits shifted off the left wrap back into the right end — no bits are lost. Common in cryptographic primitives and CRC computation.
GATE_ROR_SUMMARY: Cyclically rotates the input vector right.
GATE_ROR_DESC: Mirror of ROL — bits off the right wrap into the left.
GATE_EQ_SUMMARY: Outputs 1 when both inputs are equal.
GATE_EQ_DESC: Per-bit XNOR followed by an AND across all the bits. For 1-bit inputs, this is just an XNOR. We emit EQ cells when synthesising `case`/`with-select` statements — each `when` choice becomes an EQ comparator against the selector.
GATE_NEQ_DESC: Inverse of EQ — equivalent to a per-bit XOR followed by an OR.
GATE_LT_DESC: Magnitude comparator. Built from a chain of full-adder-style cells in hardware; we keep it as a single opaque cell.
GATE_LTE_DESC: Same family as LT, with a tweaked carry-out interpretation.
GATE_BLACKBOX_SUMMARY: A VHDL process whose body the synthesiser couldn't decompose.
GATE_BLACKBOX_DESC: Process bodies that use loops, function calls, or constructs we don't lower yet end up rendered as a single opaque cell. Inputs come from the sensitivity list; outputs are the signals the body assigns. The diagnostics row at the top of the schematic explains why each blackbox showed up.
GATE_BLACKBOX_NOTE: Future synthesiser iterations will decompose more of these — see the synthesis-coverage roadmap.
SCHEMATIC_ATTR_REASON_BLACKBOX_GENERIC: Process body uses constructs not yet decomposed (loops / function calls / etc.).

SETTINGS_PRIVACY_SUB: What Kmila stores and what leaves your device.
SETTINGS_PRIVACY_DESC: Kmila keeps your work on this device by default. Open the privacy page for the full breakdown of local storage, optional GitHub round-trips, and external resources.
PRIVACY_INTRO: Kmila is an offline-first VHDL playground. Your projects, settings, and logs stay on this device unless you explicitly choose to share them. This page lists everything stored locally, every place data can leave the device, and how to wipe or export your work.
PRIVACY_LOCAL_INTRO: Kmila uses four kinds of local storage. Nothing here is uploaded automatically.
PRIVACY_LOCAL_DB: Project database — entities, files, configurations, run snapshots. Stored in SQLite (MAUI) or IndexedDB (Web).
PRIVACY_LOCAL_SETTINGS: App settings — theme, language, text size, tick resolution, library build mode. Stored as key/value pairs in the same database.
PRIVACY_LOCAL_BUNDLES: Imported user assets — FPGA templates, language packs and VHDL libraries you bring in via Settings. Stored on disk under the app's Documents folder.
PRIVACY_LOCAL_LOGS: Diagnostic logs — runtime events kept in memory (capped buffer). Visible from the Logs viewer and never written to disk unless you export them.
PRIVACY_LOCAL_NOTE: Nothing in the lists above leaves your device on its own.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_SUB: What happens when you submit a report.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_INTRO: Kmila offers three ways to send feedback, in order of how much leaves your device. All of them are opt-in — they only run when you click their button.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_TIER1: Copy diagnostics: builds a text snapshot (app version, OS, language, log tail) and copies it to your clipboard. Nothing is uploaded.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_TIER2: Open issue URL: opens GitHub's new-issue form in your browser with the diagnostics prefilled. You still control whether to submit it.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_TIER3: Submit in-app (requires GitHub sign-in): posts the issue directly to the Kmila repository as your authenticated user. Only this tier requires authentication.
PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_NOTE: The diagnostics payload never includes your project source code or your saved files — only environment metadata and recent log lines.
PRIVACY_CDN_SUB: Third-party fonts, CDNs and remote calls.
PRIVACY_CDN_INTRO: Kmila is offline-first: vendored dependencies are bundled with the app rather than loaded from the network. A small number of resources may still be fetched on first paint, depending on how the host page is built (Web vs MAUI) — for example Monaco's worker scripts or system fonts referenced by Mermaid diagrams. None of these requests carry your project data.
PRIVACY_CDN_NOTE: If you spot a CDN reference that shouldn't be there, please report it via the feedback button on Settings — offline-first is a hard requirement.
PRIVACY_RIGHTS_SUB: How to take your projects with you, or wipe them.
PRIVACY_RIGHTS_EXPORT: Export: every project can be exported as a portable .kmila bundle from Settings → Project bundles. The bundle contains your sources, entities, configurations and any imported libraries. It is a normal file you control — copy, back up, or share it as you wish.
PRIVACY_RIGHTS_DELETE: Delete: individual projects can be removed from the Projects view; imported FPGAs, languages and libraries can be removed one at a time in Settings. To wipe everything at once, uninstall the app (MAUI) or clear site data for Kmila in your browser (Web).
PRIVACY_RIGHTS_NOTE: Kmila has no remote account database, so there is nothing for us to delete on your behalf — deletion is always done locally by you.
TUTORIAL_WELCOME_BODY: A quick 60-second tour will show you where Projects, Learn, Concepts and Settings live. You can skip it at any time and re-take it later.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTS_BODY: Start here. Create a new VHDL project, open an existing one, or import a .kmila bundle a colleague shared with you.
TUTORIAL_LEARN_BODY: Guided lessons with inline simulations: gates, flip-flops, FSMs and more. Progress is tracked locally so you can pick up where you left off.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTS_BODY: Practice block-based exercises that build intuition for concurrent and sequential thinking — no typing required.
TUTORIAL_SETTINGS_BODY: Theme, language, simulation precision, library imports, and your privacy page — all configurable from here.
TUTORIAL_FINAL_BODY: That's the tour. Everything lives on this device by default — see Settings → Privacy for the full breakdown. Have fun!
SETTINGS_TUTORIAL_HINT: Replay the guided tour on every view — and switch tours back on if you'd turned them off.
SETTINGS_TUTORIAL_RESET_DONE: Welcome tours reset — they'll fire again next time you open each view.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICE_BODY: Curated VHDL puzzles with auto-grading. Filter by difficulty or modality and track your solved count.
TUTORIAL_TOPBAR_CONFIG_BODY: When you open a project, this pill shows the active simulation configuration. Click to switch presets or create a new one.
TUTORIAL_TOPBAR_PROFILE_BODY: Account, theme, language, FPGA picker and sign-in all live behind the avatar — one anchor for everything user-scoped.
TUTORIAL_FOOTER_BODY: The footer always links to the privacy page — what's stored, what (if anything) leaves your device, and how to wipe everything.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTSVIEW_INTRO_BODY: Every project you create lands here. The cards are sorted by most-recent activity; running projects show a live progress bar.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTSVIEW_SEARCH_BODY: Type to filter the grid by name or description. The count next to the title updates as you type.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTSVIEW_CREATE_BODY: Spin up a new VHDL project. You can pick the entity name and target FPGA, or accept the defaults and tweak later.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTSVIEW_SAMPLE_BODY: Don't have anything to simulate yet? This drops in a 4-bit counter with clock + reset, ready to run.
TUTORIAL_PROJECTSVIEW_CARD_BODY: Click anywhere on the card to open the editor. The kebab menu hides rename, duplicate, export and delete actions.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_INTRO_BODY: This is where you write, simulate and inspect VHDL. The layout has three zones: code/replay on the left, dock panels at the bottom, and the run bar in between.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_VIEWS_BODY: Switch between the source editor and the step-by-step replay of the last simulation. Both can have breakpoints set from the gutter.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_CODE_BODY: Monaco-powered VHDL editor with hover docs, error markers, and gutter breakpoints. Use the split toggle to view markdown alongside code.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_RUNBAR_BODY: Set duration, clock period and target FPGA, then hit Run. Build is automatic; Pause / Step / Stop appear once a simulation is running.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_FPGA_BODY: Pick the device the design targets. The resource panel in the dock estimates LUT / FF / IO usage against this device's capacity.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_DOCK_BODY: Files, Output, Waveforms, Schematic, Flow, Resources and Runs each open in this bottom dock. Click a tab to switch; drag the grabber to resize.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_GRABBER_BODY: Drag this grabber to change the dock height; double-click to snap full / half / collapsed. The dock can hide entirely to give the code more room.
TUTORIAL_EDITOR_FINAL_BODY: Most of what you do happens here. Use the dock tabs to explore waveforms, schematics and flow diagrams after each run.
TUTORIAL_LEARNVIEW_INTRO_BODY: The Learn module groups lessons by topic — gates, sequential logic, FSMs, and more. Pick any track to start, or use the search to jump directly to a topic.
TUTORIAL_LEARNVIEW_PROGRESS_BODY: Lessons you've finished count here. Progress is saved locally per device — no account needed.
TUTORIAL_LEARNVIEW_SEARCH_BODY: Free-text search across lesson titles and module names. Helpful when you remember a term but not which track it lives in.
TUTORIAL_LEARNVIEW_TRACK_BODY: Each module is a track of related lessons. Click any card to open the lesson — most have inline simulations and animated diagrams.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTSVIEW_INTRO_BODY: Block-based exercises that build intuition for concurrent and sequential thinking. You compose circuits visually — no VHDL typing needed.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTSVIEW_TRACK_BODY: Pick a module to read its lessons and try the linked Scratch-style exercises. Completed exercises mark the module as done.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTSVIEW_SEARCH_BODY: Filter the modules below by title or topic.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEVIEW_INTRO_BODY: Hand-curated VHDL challenges with auto-grading. Solve them in any order; your solved count updates in the sidebar.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEVIEW_FILTERS_BODY: Narrow the catalog to a specific difficulty band or the exercise type you want to drill (combinational, sequential, FSM, etc.).
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEVIEW_TRACK_BODY: Each card has its statement, expected ports and a Solve button that drops you straight into a scoped editor session.
TUTORIAL_SETTINGSVIEW_INTRO_BODY: Each card is a preferences group. The page is search-and-scroll, not tabbed — everything sits on one canvas for quick scanning.
TUTORIAL_SETTINGSVIEW_APPEARANCE_BODY: Theme, language, text size and tutorial replay. Changes apply immediately — no Save button needed.
TUTORIAL_SETTINGSVIEW_SIMULATION_BODY: Tick resolution and live-replay capture. Defaults are sensible — only touch these if you hit aliasing or memory limits.
TUTORIAL_SETTINGSVIEW_PRIVACY_BODY: Opens the full privacy page: local-storage inventory, how feedback round-trips through GitHub, and how to export or delete your data.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_INTRO_BODY: Wire real-looking switches, LEDs and displays to your design's signals, then watch them react as the simulation runs — no waveforms required.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_TOOLBAR_BODY: Run, wire, undo, zoom and export all live up here. The controls that only matter mid-run appear once you press Run.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_PALETTE_BODY: Drag inputs, LEDs, displays and actuators onto the canvas from here. They're grouped by family so you can find one fast.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_CANVAS_BODY: Drop widgets here and arrange them freely. Pan and zoom to lay out a tidy little front panel for your circuit.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_WIRE_BODY: Turn on wiring mode to bind each widget's pins to your entity's ports, so the simulation can drive and read them.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_RUN_BODY: Press Run to start simulating. Your switches become live inputs and the displays update in real time; press again to stop.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_EXPORT_BODY: Behind this menu you can fit the view to screen, list every widget, and export the canvas as PNG, SVG or PDF — or record it as a video.
TUTORIAL_VISUAL_FINAL_BODY: That's the visual simulator. Add a few widgets, wire them up and hit Run to see your design come to life.
TUTORIAL_LESSON_INTRO_BODY: Each lesson mixes a short read with live diagrams and simulations you can play with as you go.
TUTORIAL_LESSON_BODY_BODY: Read through here. Many lessons embed animated gates, timing diagrams or a runnable sample you can open in the editor.
TUTORIAL_LESSON_COMPLETE_BODY: Done with the lesson? Mark it complete to track your progress — you can always undo it later.
TUTORIAL_LESSON_NAV_BODY: Jump to the previous or next lesson in the track from here, without going back to the list.
TUTORIAL_LESSON_FINAL_BODY: That's a lesson. Work through the track at your own pace — your progress is saved on this device.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTLESSON_INTRO_BODY: Concept lessons build intuition with visuals and a replayable example, instead of code you have to type.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTLESSON_BODY_BODY: The lesson text sits here, often with an embedded step-through player that animates the idea as it runs.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTLESSON_COMPLETE_BODY: Mark the concept done when you've got it — it counts toward the module's progress and can be undone anytime.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTLESSON_NAV_BODY: Move to the neighbouring concepts in this module straight from the footer.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTEXERCISE_INTRO_BODY: Compose a small circuit from blocks — no VHDL typing. Snap the pieces together, run it, and see whether it behaves.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTEXERCISE_WORKSPACE_BODY: Drag blocks into this area and connect them. This is where you build your answer to the exercise.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTEXERCISE_RUN_BODY: Press Run to simulate what you built. You'll get a friendly hint if a combination isn't recognised yet.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTEXERCISE_COMPLETE_BODY: Once the exercise checks out, mark it complete to record it against the module.
TUTORIAL_CONCEPTEXERCISE_FINAL_BODY: That's a block exercise. Build, run and iterate until the result matches what's asked.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEEX_INTRO_BODY: A self-contained VHDL puzzle with automatic grading. Read the brief, write your solution, and submit to see how it scores.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEEX_BRIEF_BODY: The statement, the expected ports and the visible test case live here — plus your results once you submit.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEEX_EDITOR_BODY: This editor comes seeded with a starter. Fill in the logic; it's a focused, single-file workspace scoped to this challenge.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEEX_SUBMIT_BODY: Hit Submit to run your code against every test case. You'll get a verdict and, once solved, the full solution to compare against.
TUTORIAL_PRACTICEEX_FINAL_BODY: That's a practice challenge. Solve them in any order — your solved count grows in the sidebar.
TUTORIAL_LOGS_INTRO_BODY: Every event the app records shows up here — handy for understanding what happened, especially on mobile where there's no console.
TUTORIAL_LOGS_SEARCH_BODY: Filter entries by any text in the message or category. The count by the title updates as you type.
TUTORIAL_LOGS_LEVEL_BODY: Narrow the list to just Info, Warning or Error when you're chasing something specific.
TUTORIAL_LOGS_EXPORT_BODY: Save the current entries to a file — useful to attach when you report a bug.
TUTORIAL_LOGS_CLEAR_BODY: Wipe the in-memory buffer to start fresh. Capture keeps running in the background.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_INTRO_BODY: This page is the honest breakdown of what Kmila stores, where it lives, and what — if anything — ever leaves your device.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_LOCAL_BODY: Your projects, progress and settings are kept locally in your browser or app — not on a server by default.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_FEEDBACK_BODY: If you send feedback or a diagnostic report, this explains exactly what's included and how it travels through GitHub.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_CDN_BODY: The few outside resources Kmila loads — like fonts and libraries from CDNs — are listed here so there are no surprises.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_RIGHTS_BODY: It's your data: this section shows how to export everything or wipe it completely whenever you want.
TUTORIAL_PRIVACY_FINAL_BODY: That's the privacy picture. Anything stored is yours to export or delete from Settings at any time.
SETTINGS_EDITOR_SYNC_MODE_HINT: Automatic keeps the two views in sync on every tab switch. Manual only updates the other view when you Save.
SETTINGS_ADVANCED_MODE_HINT: Show the expert widget bindings in the Visual editor. Off by default — beginners wire the real device pins only.
SETTINGS_ADVANCED_MODE_WARN: Expert bindings use high-level ports the simulator fills in for you. A design that works with them can still fail on a real FPGA, because the hardware was never fully described. Not recommended if you're new to VHDL.

EXAMPLE_CAPSTONE_DESC: Full 32-bit CPU calculator with keypad, LCD, 4-digit 7-seg, LED matrix, and buzzer. 16 VHDL files.
EXAMPLE_FULLADDER_DESC: A full adder built from two half adders plus an OR gate, linked with port map. The first multi-file structural example.
EXAMPLE_RIPPLE4_DESC: Four full adders chained so each carry ripples into the next — a three-level hierarchy (adder → full adder → half adder).
EXAMPLE_MUX4_DESC: A 4-to-1 mux built structurally from three 2-to-1 mux blocks. Flip the select lines to route one input to the output.
EXAMPLE_CMP4_DESC: Four 1-bit comparator slices cascaded from the most significant bit to tell whether A > B, A = B, or A < B.

SATISFACTION_BODY: Got a minute? A short survey helps us improve Kmila.
SATISFACTION_BODY_AGAIN: Thanks for your feedback! Want to share more?
PRIVACY_KMILA_INTRO: Kmila can open pages on kmila.com.mx in your browser. The app itself never sends any data — your browser makes the request, and only if you choose to submit the form.
PRIVACY_KMILA_REPORT: Bug report form (opens pre-filled with diagnostics you can review before sending)
PRIVACY_KMILA_SURVEY: Satisfaction survey (anonymous or with your account)
PRIVACY_KMILA_NOTE: These are external links only. Nothing is transmitted in the background — opening a link hands off to your browser, exactly like the GitHub feedback path.
EDITOR_EMPTY_SOURCE_CONTROL: Link a GitHub repository to track this project.
VC_UNAVAILABLE_DEMO: Source control isn't available in the demo.
VC_SIGN_IN_PROMPT: Sign in to GitHub to use source control.
VC_NOT_LINKED_BODY: Link this project to a GitHub repository to track changes, commit and push.
VC_LINK_CONFIRM_BODY: Linking adopts the repository's contents as the baseline — local files may be overwritten or added. Continue?
VC_CREATE_PRIVATE_HINT: Enable 'private-repo access' in Settings to create private repositories.
VC_AUTOCOMMIT_HINT: Automatically commit and push each save (this project only).
VC_UNLINK_CONFIRM_BODY: This removes the link and local snapshot. Your files and the GitHub repository are not affected.
VC_NEEDS_PULL_BODY: The repository has new commits. Pull them, then commit?
VC_CONFLICT_BODY: You have local changes and the repository has new commits. Pull anyway and overwrite your local changes?
VC_OUT_NEEDSPULL: Pull first — the repository has new commits.
VC_OUT_CONFLICT: Local changes conflict with new remote commits.
VC_OUT_RATELIMITED: GitHub rate limit — try again shortly.
SETTINGS_VC_PRIVATE_HINT: Request the wider 'repo' scope so source control can use private repositories. Takes effect on your next sign-in.
SETTINGS_VC_PRIVATE_REAUTH: Sign out and back in for the new scope to take effect.
PRIVACY_VC_NOTE: Source control (optional): when you link a project, Kmila pushes/pulls to your own GitHub repository — only on explicit actions or per-project auto-commit. Nothing else is sent.
WASM_SIM_BODY: The browser demo runs the whole simulator on a single thread, so this page pauses until the run finishes. For a smoother, faster experience, use the desktop app.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_SUB: Serve /api/v1 from this app so SimulatorBench or curl can drive it.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_ENABLE_HINT: Starts a Kestrel host on 127.0.0.1 (or LAN, see below).
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_UNSUPPORTED: Not available on iOS in this release.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_PORT_HINT: Default 5298 matches SimulatorBench's fallback. Use 0 to let the OS pick.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_LAN_HINT: Binds 0.0.0.0 so other devices on your network can reach the API. Loopback is safer.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_LAN_WARN: Anyone on your local network can hit this port. Set an auth token below to gate access.
SETTINGS_LOCALAPI_TOKEN_HINT: Optional bearer token. Empty = unauthenticated (dev default).
